ety.text: From Middle English gate (the forms ȝate and ȝeat yielded the dialectal doublet yate), from the plural of Old English ġeat (specifically gatu), from Proto-West Germanic *gat, from Proto-Germanic *gatą (“hole, opening”). See also Old Norse gat, Swedish and Dutch gat, Low German Gaat, Gööt.
Borrowed from Old Norse gata, from Proto-Germanic *gatwǭ. Cognate with Danish gade, Swedish gata, German Gasse (“lane”). Doublet of gait.

senses.d: A doorlike structure outside a house.
A doorway, opening, or passage in a fence or wall.
A movable barrier.
ex: The gate in front of the railroad crossing went up after the train had passed.

senses.d: A passageway (as in an air terminal) where passengers can embark or disembark.
A location which serves as a conduit for transport, migration, or trade.
The amount of money made by selling tickets to a concert or a sports event.
A logical pathway made up of switches which turn on or off. Examples are and, or, nand, etc.
The controlling terminal of a field effect transistor (FET).
In a lock tumbler, the opening for the stump of the bolt to pass through or into.
The channel or opening through which metal is poured into the mould; the ingate; tedge.
To keep something inside by means of a closed gate.
To punish (a student) by not allowing to leave the college grounds.
ex: You climbed the wall, for which you ought to be gated; and finally, you came in blotto, for which you ought to be sent down.

“I’ve missed two lectures already,” remarked Maurice, who was breakfasting in his pyjamas.
“Cut them all — he’ll only gate you.”

senses.d: To open (a closed ion channel).

ex: Access to the building is gated by a security system.

senses.d: A way, path.

senses.d: To collect normally separate things.

senses.d: To accumulate over time, to amass little by little.
ex: Over the years he'd gathered a considerable collection of mugs.

senses.d: To congregate, or assemble.
ex: People gathered round as he began to tell his story.
Tears from the depth of some divine despair / Rise in the heart, and gather to the eyes, […]

senses.d: To grow gradually larger by accretion.
ex: Their snow-ball did not gather as it went.

senses.d: To bring parts of a whole closer.
ex: She gathered the shawl about her as she stepped into the cold.

senses.d: To add pleats or folds to a piece of cloth, normally to reduce its width.
ex: A gown should be gathered around the top so that it will remain shaped.

senses.d: To bring stitches closer together.
ex: Be careful not to stretch or gather your knitting.
If you want to emphasise the shape, it is possible to gather the waistline.
